title: Security Essentials (020-100) practice exam
note: Original questions written for MyNextCert from LPI's public Security Essentials 020-100 objectives, version 1.0 (https://www.lpi.org/twbm, checked 2026-11-26). Not real exam questions. Domains 1.0 to 5.0 here are LPI topics 021 to 025, and objective 1.1 is LPI 021.1, and so on. The weights follow LPI's objective weights (12, 23, 22, 25 and 18 percent of the 40 items). The real exam is 40 questions in 60 minutes; this pool is larger so each attempt differs, and it includes 4 hands-on items (3 per full exam).

q.q: A hospital's records system is locked by ransomware, and nurses cannot open any patient chart. No data was copied out and none was changed. Which security goal took the main hit?
o: Confidentiality
Confidentiality means only the right people can read the data. Nothing was read or copied here.
Availability
Right. The data is intact and private, but the people who need it cannot reach it.
Integrity
Integrity means the data stays accurate and unaltered. The charts were not changed, only blocked.
Non-repudiation
Non-repudiation means a person cannot deny an action they took. It is about proof, not access.

q.q: A teenager with no coding skill downloads a ready-made attack tool and runs it against a school website to impress friends. Which description fits this actor best?
o: A state-sponsored group running a long, planned campaign
Nation-state groups are well funded and patient. A teenager showing off is not that.
A malicious insider abusing access they were given
An insider already has legitimate access. This person is attacking from outside.
A competitor stealing trade secrets for profit
Industrial spying is planned and aimed at secrets. Nothing here points to it.
A low-skill attacker using tools others wrote
Right. The tool does the work, and the motive is showing off, not money or politics.

q.q: A manager signs a contract with a digital signature. Later she claims she never agreed. Which goal does a valid signature protect that makes this claim fail?
o: Availability, because the file is always reachable
Availability is about access to data. A signature does not keep a file online.
Non-repudiation
Right. Only her private key could make that signature, so she cannot credibly deny it.
Confidentiality, because the text is hidden from others
A signature does not hide the text. Hiding it takes encryption.
Anonymity, because the signer stays unknown
A signature does the opposite: it ties the document to a known person.

q.q: Your unit uses a small office router. Where is the best place to learn whether a known flaw in its firmware has a fix?
o: A forum post from an unknown user claiming to have fixed it
Unverified posts may be wrong or even harmful. Use the maker and the CVE list.
The router's own login page
The login page does not list flaws. It may not even show the firmware version.
The router's packaging
The box shows nothing about flaws found after it was printed.
The vendor's advisory and the CVE entry
Right. Vendors publish advisories with fixed versions, and CVE numbers give each flaw a shared name.

q.q: Which of these is a vulnerability and not an incident?
o: A stranger signed in to a staff account and read mail
This is an incident: harm already happened.
A server missing a patch for a known flaw
Right. It is a weakness that could be used. Nothing bad has happened yet.
A laptop that was stolen from a car
This is an incident: a loss event already occurred.
Ransomware that encrypted a shared drive
This is an incident: the attack succeeded.

q.q: A forensic examiner receives a suspect laptop. What should she do first?
o: Boot it and browse the files to look for clues
Booting changes the disk and timestamps, which spoils evidence.
Run a cleanup tool to remove junk files
Cleanup deletes data that may be evidence.
Make a bit-for-bit copy and examine the copy
Right. The original stays unchanged, so the evidence can be trusted and the work repeated.
Reinstall the operating system
Reinstalling wipes the evidence the examiner needs.

q.q: A company writes down who leads, who talks to staff and what steps to follow when a breach happens. What is this document?
o: An incident response plan
Right. It names the roles and steps so the team does not improvise during a crisis.
A vulnerability scan report
A scan report lists weaknesses found. It does not assign roles for a breach.
A backup rotation schedule
A schedule says when backups run. It is not a breach plan.
An acceptable use policy
This tells staff what they may do with IT. It does not direct a response team.

q.q: You are curious about a neighbor company's website, so after work you run a port scanner against it. You have no permission, and you plan to just look. What is the best way to see this?
o: It is fine because the website is public and anyone can visit it
A public web page does not mean its servers can be probed.
It is fine if you do not change anything
Many laws cover unauthorized access and probing, not just damage.
It is fine if you do it after work hours
The time of day does not matter. Authorization does.
It may be illegal, since you need written permission first
Right. Scanning other people's systems without authorization can break the law. Good intent is not a defense.

q.q: You find a flaw in a vendor's mobile app while using it. What is the most responsible next step?
o: Post full details online at once so everyone is warned
Posting an unfixed flaw hands attackers a roadmap.
Test the flaw on other users' accounts to prove it works
Using it on real users' data is unauthorized and harmful.
Tell the vendor privately and allow time to fix it
Right. Private reporting protects users while the fix is made.
Keep quiet and delete the app
Silence leaves other users exposed.

q.q: While fixing a printer, a help desk technician notices a spreadsheet of coworkers' medical leave on the shared drive. What should the technician do?
o: Leave it alone and tell the owner or security team
Right. Access to fix a printer is not permission to use private data. Reporting the exposure helps the owner fix it.
Copy it to a USB drive to keep it safe
Copying private data spreads it and is not part of the job.
Tell a few friends so staff can all be more careful about it
Passing on private information causes the harm the technician should prevent.
Delete the file so nobody else sees it
Deleting data you do not own may destroy records.

q.q: A unit cannot move its data center out of a flood zone, so it buys insurance that pays for flood losses. Which risk treatment is this?
o: Risk acceptance
Acceptance means living with the risk and its cost. Paying for insurance does something about it.
Risk transfer
Right. The financial loss is shifted to the insurer, though the flood risk itself still exists.
Risk avoidance
Avoidance would mean not operating in the flood zone at all.
Risk mitigation by hardening the servers
Mitigation reduces the likelihood or impact directly, for example with raised racks. Insurance only pays afterward.

q.q: A website uses a public-key exchange to agree on a secret, then encrypts the page data with that secret. Which term describes this mix?
o: Pure symmetric encryption only
Symmetric alone needs a safe way to share the key first. The exchange step is asymmetric.
Hybrid cryptography
Right. Asymmetric methods set up a session key. Fast symmetric encryption then protects the data.
Hashing
A hash is a one-way fingerprint. It cannot be reversed to decrypt data.
Steganography
This hides data inside other files. It is not how TLS works.

q.q: A download page lists a SHA-256 value next to the file. After downloading, you compute the same value and it matches. What does the match show?
o: The file is free of malware
A match only says the file is unchanged. The original could itself be bad.
The file is encrypted
A hash does not encrypt anything.
The file is unchanged from the one that was hashed
Right. A hash is a fingerprint of the exact bytes. The match is a check on integrity.
The download came from a site with a CA-signed certificate
The hash says nothing about where the file came from.

q.q: What does perfect forward secrecy (PFS) give you?
o: Past sessions stay private even if the server's long-term private key is stolen later
Right. Each session uses its own temporary key, so one stolen key cannot open old recordings.
Faster page loads on every visit
PFS adds a little work. It is not a speed feature.
A guarantee that the server is trusted
Trust comes from certificates, not PFS.
Protection from all malware on the server
PFS protects recorded traffic, not the server itself.

q.q: A company learns that the private key of its web certificate was stolen. What lets browsers learn that the certificate should no longer be trusted?
o: A longer password on the web server's admin account
A password does not cancel a certificate that already exists.
Clearing the browser's history
History has nothing to do with certificate trust.
Changing the site's IP address
Certificates are tied to names and keys. A new IP does not revoke anything.
Revocation, through a CRL or an OCSP check
Right. The CA marks the certificate as revoked, and clients can look this up.

q.q: Which statement about a private key in public-key cryptography is correct?
o: It stays secret with its owner. The public key is shared
Right. Anyone can use the public key, but only the owner's private key can decrypt or sign.
It is sent to the CA with every certificate request
The CA only needs the public key. Sending a private key would defeat its purpose.
It is published inside the certificate so that everyone can verify it
The certificate holds the public key, never the private one.
Two people should always share it
Sharing breaks the link to one owner. Signatures would mean nothing.

q.q: A browser shows 'The certificate is for a different name than the site you are visiting.' What does this warning mean?
o: The certificate was issued for another domain, so the connection may not be to the real site
Right. A certificate must match the name in the address bar. A mismatch can be a mistake or an interception.
The site's server has run out of disk space
Disk space is not part of a certificate check.
Your device clock is always wrong
A bad clock can cause expiry warnings, but this one is about the name.
The site uses a stronger cipher than your browser
Cipher strength does not trigger a name warning.

q.q: A site shows a padlock and HTTPS. What does the padlock tell you?
o: The company behind the site is honest
A padlock says nothing about honesty.
The site has no malware
Malware and encryption are separate issues.
Your device is free of viruses
Your device is not checked by a site's padlock.
The connection is encrypted and the certificate matches the site name, but the site may still be harmful
Right. HTTPS protects data in transit. Criminals can get certificates for their own lookalike sites.

q.q: A small club wants a free, trusted certificate for its site that renews itself. Which CA fits?
o: A self-signed certificate made on the club's server
Browsers do not trust self-signed certificates, and visitors see a warning.
A certificate bought from a commercial CA with a 3-year term
A commercial CA is trusted, but it is not free and a 3-year term does not renew itself. It does not match the club's needs.
A certificate from the user's own laptop CA
A private CA is not in browsers' trust lists, so visitors would see warnings.
Let's Encrypt
Right. It is a free CA that issues short-lived domain certificates and supports automatic renewal.

q.q: Maria wants to send Ana an encrypted OpenPGP email that only Ana can read. Which key does Maria need?
o: Ana's private key
A private key is never shared. If Maria had it, Ana's secrecy would be gone.
Maria's private key
Maria's private key makes signatures. It does not make mail readable only by Ana.
Ana's public key
Right. Data encrypted with Ana's public key can only be opened with Ana's private key.
A hash of the message
A hash is a fingerprint. It does not hide the message.

q.q: A user wants the reader of an email to be sure it came from her and was not edited on the way. What should she add?
o: Encryption with her public key
This would only let her read it back. It proves nothing about who sent it.
A longer subject line
The subject line is not protected and can be changed.
A read receipt
A receipt shows opening. It does not prove the sender or the content.
A digital signature
Right. The reader checks it with her public key. Any change to the message breaks the check.

q.q: How does S/MIME decide that a public key belongs to a given email address?
o: Members of the public vote on each key
S/MIME does not vote. OpenPGP is the one that uses personal trust.
The mail server picks a random key
A random pick links nothing to a person.
The mail client reads it from the plain-text message header
A header is plain text anyone can edit.
A CA-issued certificate tying the key to the address
Right. S/MIME uses a CA-signed X.509 certificate for this link.

q.q: A laptop with confidential files is left on a train. The drive was protected with full-disk encryption (BitLocker) and a strong PIN. Why is the data likely safe?
o: The laptop will lock itself and call the police
BitLocker does not alert anyone. It protects the data on the drive.
Encryption prevents the laptop from being stolen
Encryption protects data, not the device.
Without the key, the drive's contents look like random data even if the disk is moved to another computer
Right. Encryption at rest protects the files when the device falls into the wrong hands.
The data was automatically copied to the cloud
Encryption does not copy data. That is backup.

q.q: What is a VeraCrypt container?
o: A hardware chip on the motherboard
This describes a TPM. A container is a file.
One encrypted file that appears as a drive when mounted
Right. You open it, work with files as on a normal drive and dismount to lock it.
A cloud service that scans stored files for malware and viruses
VeraCrypt is a local encryption tool, not a scanner.
A kind of USB cable that blocks data
That is a data blocker. It has no link to a container.

q.q: A team syncs files with a cloud service but does not want the provider to read them. Which tool fits?
o: Cryptomator, which encrypts files before they sync
Right. The provider only stores encrypted data, and the key stays with the team.
A screen saver with a password
A screen lock does not protect files stored at the provider.
A larger cloud storage plan
More space does not add secrecy.
A second cloud account at another provider with the same files
A copy at another provider is just another place the files can be read.

q.q: An employee finds a USB drive in the parking lot with a label 'Payroll 2026'. What is the safest action?
o: Plug it into a home computer to find the owner
A personal computer can be infected, and it may carry the problem into your network later.
Plug it in with antivirus running
Some malware runs the moment a drive is attached, before a scan can help.
Format it and keep it
Formatting does not make an unknown device trustworthy and keeping it has no benefit.
Do not plug it in. Give it to IT or security
Right. Dropped drives are a known trick to deliver malware. IT can check it safely.

q.q: A smart camera still uses its factory password and has never been updated. What is the biggest risk, and the best first fix?
o: The picture is slightly blurry. Move the camera closer
This is not a security risk.
It uses too much power. Unplug it at night
Power use is not the concern, and unplugging does not fix a weak login.
It will lose Wi-Fi. Add a second router
A second router does not secure the camera.
It can be taken over, perhaps joining a botnet. Change the password and update the firmware
Right. Default passwords are well known, and old firmware has known flaws.

q.q: What does a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) do in a computer?
o: Speeds up the graphics card
Graphics work is done by the GPU.
Scans files for viruses
Scanning is done by security software, not the TPM.
Blocks all USB devices
A TPM does not control USB ports.
Stores keys in hardware and helps check that the boot process was not tampered with
Right. Tools like BitLocker use it to keep keys safe from software attacks.

q.q: You need a free PDF editor. Which choice is safest?
o: The first search result on a download aggregator site
Aggregators often wrap installers with unwanted or harmful extras.
Get it from the maker's official site or the platform's own store and check it if a hash is given
Right. Official sources keep the risk of tampered or bundled malware low.
A link a stranger sent in a chat
Unknown links are a common way to deliver malware.
A cracked version from a file-sharing site
Cracked software often carries hidden malware.

q.q: Why should you install operating system and application updates promptly?
o: They always add new features that you absolutely must have
Some updates add features, but the security reason matters most.
They erase old data to free space
Updates do not wipe your data.
They fix known flaws attackers already use
Right. Once a flaw is public, attacks follow quickly. Patching closes the opening.
They make the device unhackable
No update does this. Updates reduce risk.

q.q: A web login form accepts the text ' OR 1=1 -- as a username and lets the tester in. What flaw does this show?
o: A weak Wi-Fi password
This is a web app flaw, not a wireless one.
A missing backup
Backups are not related to logging in without credentials.
SQL injection, from unchecked user input
Right. The input became part of the database query. Input must be validated and queries parameterized.
An expired certificate on the login page's server
A certificate does not stop the form from reading its input as code.

q.q: A threat spreads from computer to computer across a network by itself, using an unpatched flaw, without anyone opening a file. What is it?
o: A virus
A virus attaches to a file or program and needs someone to run it.
A keylogger
A keylogger records typing and does not spread itself.
A worm
Right. Worms replicate and move on their own. Viruses need a host file and a user action.
Adware
Adware shows unwanted ads and does not spread across a network by itself.

q.q: What makes a rootkit especially hard to find?
o: It always shows a ransom note
A ransom note is ransomware's trait, not a rootkit's.
It only runs while the computer is switched off completely
Malware needs the computer on to run.
It sends many loud pop-ups
Pop-ups are easy to spot. Rootkits aim to hide.
It hides its files and processes from normal tools
Right. It can make normal tools show a clean system.

q.q: A flashlight app on a phone asks to read your contacts and send texts. What is the likely risk?
o: The battery will charge faster
A permission request does not change charging.
It may be spyware that steals the address book and uses it to spam or phish your contacts
Right. A flashlight needs neither permission. Excess permissions are a warning sign.
The camera flash will stop working
This is not a security concern.
The app will update itself less often
Update frequency does not explain the permissions.

q.q: A new malware strain was released yesterday. Why might signature-based antivirus miss it?
o: Antivirus only scans on Mondays
Scans can run at any time. The gap is about knowledge of the threat.
Its signature is not in the database yet
Right. Signatures only match known samples. Keep the tool updated and use behavior detection too.
Signature databases are never updated by any vendor
Vendors update them often, but a new threat comes first.
Antivirus cannot read PDF files
The tool can read many file types. The new threat is the problem.

q.q: A unit makes a full backup on Sunday, then an incremental backup each night. The disk fails on Thursday morning. Which backups are needed to restore?
o: Only Wednesday's incremental
Wednesday's backup holds just that day's changes.
Sunday's full backup plus Monday to Wednesday incrementals
Right. Each incremental holds only changes since the last backup, so the restore needs the full copy and every incremental after it.
Only Sunday's full backup
This would lose three days of work.
Wednesday's and Tuesday's incrementals only, without any full copy
Without the full backup there is nothing to apply them to.

q.q: What does the 3-2-1 backup rule recommend?
o: Three copies, two media types, one copy off site
Right. This way one event such as fire or theft cannot destroy every copy.
Three backups a day, two weeks of history, one password
The numbers in the rule refer to copies, media and place.
Three people, two locks, one safe
This describes physical security, not backup copies.
Three drives of the same type kept together
Same media in one place shares the same risks.

q.q: A user relies on a cloud sync folder as her only backup. Ransomware encrypts files on her laptop. What happens?
o: The cloud will undo the changes automatically
Basic sync does not know a change is harmful, and some services keep versions only for a short time.
The encrypted files may sync up and replace the good copies, so sync is not a backup
Right. Sync mirrors changes, good or bad. A true backup keeps older versions apart.
The cloud will not accept changed files
Sync accepts changes as normal.
The cloud will warn the FBI
Providers do not do this when files sync.

q.q: A firewall rule must allow staff to open encrypted websites. Which destination port and protocol does it need?
o: TCP 23 (Telnet)
Port 23 is Telnet, which sends data in clear text.
TCP 443
Right. HTTPS uses TCP port 443.
UDP 53
Port 53 is DNS lookups.
TCP 25
Port 25 carries email between mail servers.

q.q: A user can open a site by typing its IP address but not by typing its name. Which service is the likely problem?
o: DNS, the name lookup service
Right. The path works, but the name lookup fails.
DHCP, which hands out addresses
If DHCP failed, the user would have no working address and could not reach the IP either.
NTP, which sets the clock
A wrong clock does not stop name lookups.
ARP, which finds local MAC addresses
ARP failure would also block reaching the IP address.

q.q: What is true about a MAC address compared with an IP address?
o: A MAC address changes every time a packet crosses a router
The MAC is tied to the network card. Routers rewrite the frame addressing per hop but the card keeps its address.
A MAC address identifies a network card on the local link, while IP addresses are used to route between networks
Right. MAC addresses are used on the same local network. Routers use IP addresses to cross networks.
A MAC address is chosen by your ISP
Manufacturers set the MAC. Your ISP assigns addresses at the IP layer.
A MAC address is the same as a port number
A port number picks a service. A MAC picks a card.

q.q: A developer uploads code to a provider that handles the servers, operating system and runtime, and the developer manages only the app. Which cloud model is this?
o: IaaS (infrastructure as a service)
With IaaS the customer manages the operating system and above.
SaaS (software as a service)
With SaaS you just use finished software and do not upload your own code.
PaaS (platform as a service)
Right. The provider runs the platform and the customer supplies the application.
On-premises hosting
On-premises means the organization owns and runs the hardware.

q.q: Which device forwards traffic between different IP networks, such as a home network and the Internet?
o: A switch
A basic switch moves frames inside one local network using MAC addresses.
A hub
A hub repeats signals to every port and does not route.
A router
Right. Routers read IP addresses and pick the next hop between networks.
A patch panel
A patch panel is just a set of cable connections.

q.q: Which home Wi-Fi setting gives the best protection?
o: WPA2 or WPA3 with a long, unique passphrase
Right. Modern encryption and a strong passphrase make eavesdropping and guessing hard.
WEP with a short key
WEP can be broken in minutes.
An open network with a hidden name
Hiding the name does not encrypt traffic.
WPA2 but with the default passphrase on the label
Default phrases on routers can be guessed or looked up for certain models.

q.q: A traveler uses an open Wi-Fi hotspot at a cafe to check work email. Which risk is greatest, and what helps?
o: The signal will be too slow. Move seats
Speed is not a security risk.
The cafe will charge for the email. Pay in cash
Email use over Wi-Fi is not billed per message.
The email provider will close the account. Use a nickname
Providers do not close accounts for using public Wi-Fi.
Others can intercept traffic. Use a trusted VPN
Right. On open Wi-Fi anyone nearby can try to eavesdrop or sit in the middle.

q.q: Thousands of infected home devices are told by one attacker to send traffic to a company website at the same moment, and the site goes down. What is this?
o: A DDoS from a botnet
Right. Many compromised devices flood the target so real users cannot get in.
A man-in-the-middle attack
This attack sits between two parties. Here the goal is to overload.
A phishing campaign
Phishing tricks people. Here the traffic floods a server.
A password spray
This tries common passwords. It does not flood a site.

q.q: A packet filter is set to block all inbound traffic to TCP port 23. What does it decide on?
o: Header details such as addresses, port and protocol
Right. Basic packet filtering looks at headers, not the meaning of the content.
The meaning of the words in the sender's email message
Packet filters do not read mail content.
The user's job role
Roles are not in packet headers.
The age of the operating system
The filter cannot see the OS version.

q.q: Someone plugs a personal laptop into an unused wall jack in a lobby, and it gets full access to the internal network. Which control would best prevent this?
o: A louder Wi-Fi password
The attack came through a wired jack.
A screen saver that locks the lobby computers more often
Screen savers protect unattended screens, not network ports.
Disable unused ports and require 802.1X
Right. This stops unknown devices from joining the wired network.
Turn off the lobby Wi-Fi at night
Wi-Fi is wireless. Switching it off does not touch the wired wall jack, so the laptop could still plug in.

q.q: What does a VPN do on a public network?
o: Makes you fully anonymous to every site
Sites may still know you from logins and browser details.
Encrypts traffic between your device and the VPN server, hiding it from others on that network
Right. People on the same Wi-Fi cannot read the tunnel. The VPN operator can see the traffic that leaves the server.
Removes malware from your device
A VPN protects traffic. It does not clean a device.
Doubles your Internet speed
A VPN adds work and usually slows the link slightly.

q.q: How does Tor make it hard to link a user to the sites they visit?
o: It sends everything through one trusted company
One company would see both ends. Tor uses several relays.
It deletes your IP address from the Internet
Your address still exists. Tor only hides it from the destination.
Traffic passes through several relays, and no single relay knows both who you are and where you go
Right. Layered encryption means each relay knows only the step before and after it.
It scans sites and blocks harmful ones
Tor is for routing, not blocking sites.

q.q: What is the main difference between transport encryption and end-to-end encryption in a chat service?
o: With transport encryption the service can read messages, while with end-to-end only the two users can
Right. In end-to-end encryption the keys stay on the users' devices.
Transport encryption is never used on the Internet
HTTPS is transport encryption, and it is everywhere.
End-to-end encryption deletes the messages after reading
Disappearing messages are a separate feature.
They are the same, only named differently
They differ in who holds the keys.

q.q: A web proxy is set in a browser. What does a normal proxy do?
o: Sends your requests for you, so sites see its address
Right. The proxy can hide your address from the site, but it can see your requests and may not encrypt them.
Encrypts all of your device's traffic by default using strong keys
A basic proxy does not encrypt traffic. A VPN or HTTPS does.
Removes viruses from downloaded files
Some proxies filter content, but a plain proxy is just a relay.
Gives you a faster network card
A proxy is software on the path, not hardware.

q.q: A company logs which files each user opened and when. Which part of AAA is this?
o: Authentication
Authentication proves who you are, for example with a password.
Authorization
Authorization decides what you are allowed to do.
Accounting
Right. Accounting records what was done and by whom.
Availability
Availability is a security goal, not one of the AAA parts.

q.q: Which sign-in uses two different kinds of factors?
o: A password plus a phone authenticator code
Right. One factor is something you know and the other is something you have.
A password plus a PIN
Both are things you know, so they count as one kind.
A password plus a security question about your first pet
Both are knowledge, so this is single-factor.
Two different passwords
Two passwords still make one factor.

q.q: How should a well-built service store user passwords?
o: In plain text so support can help users
Plain text hands attackers every password if the database leaks.
Encrypted with one key kept next to the data
The key and the data can be stolen together. Hashing needs no key.
In the browser's local storage
Storing them in the user's browser leaves the server nothing to check against.
As a salted, slow hash, not as readable text
Right. If the database leaks, the stolen values are hard to turn back into passwords.

q.q: An attacker takes email-and-password pairs leaked from one site and tries them on a bank site. What is this called, and what helps most?
o: Credential stuffing. Use unique passwords
Right. Reused passwords are what make it work. Unique passwords stop the chain.
Phishing. Delete the browser's cookies
Phishing tricks a person. Here the attacker uses existing passwords.
A denial of service. Buy a bigger bandwidth plan
This is login guessing, not flooding.
A rootkit install. Reinstall the OS
The attack does not touch the user's device.

q.q: Why are 'What was your first pet's name?' security questions a weak way to recover an account?
o: They take too long to type
The speed of typing is not the main risk.
They are easy to find or guess from public posts
Right. Treat answers as passwords: use random text kept in a password manager.
They are too long for most websites
Sites usually accept them. The problem is guessability.
They force users to change the answers every single month
They are not forced to change. The weakness is that they can be found.

q.q: An email says 'Your mailbox is full, sign in now' and links to mail-support-help.example. What should you do?
o: Do not click. Report it and go to the real site yourself
Right. The urgent tone and odd domain are phishing signs.
Click the link and change your password right away to be safe
The link could lead to a fake page that steals the new password.
Reply and ask for more details
Replying tells the sender your address is active.
Forward it to coworkers as a warning
Forwarding spreads the lure. Report it to security instead.

q.q: A message that looks like it is from your commander asks you to buy gift cards today and send the codes, and says not to call. Which tactic is this?
o: A routine supply request. Buy the cards
Real requests do not forbid checking.
Social engineering that uses authority and urgency. Confirm through another channel
Right. The attacker pressures you not to verify. Call the person using a number you already know.
A hardware fault in your mail client
It is a message trick, not a fault.
A malware scan result
A scan result does not ask for money.

q.q: An unexpected 'invoice.docm' arrives and asks you to 'Enable Content' to view it. What is the best action?
o: Enable it, since your antivirus program is installed and up to date
Antivirus does not catch every malicious macro.
Open it on a coworker's computer instead
This only moves the risk to someone else.
Do not enable it. Confirm with the sender or report it
Right. Macros can run code. Enabling content is how many infections start.
Rename it to .txt and open it
Renaming does not make a macro file safe or readable.

q.q: Many sites load the same advertising company's cookie. What privacy risk does that create?
o: The sites can read each other's saved passwords and logins
Cookies from an ad company do not give sites your passwords.
The cookie encrypts your hard drive
Cookies are small text files and do not encrypt anything.
The cookie turns off HTTPS
A cookie has no control over HTTPS.
The ad company can follow you across those sites
Right. A third-party cookie links your activity across different sites.

q.q: Under rules like the GDPR, which right can a person use with a company that holds their data?
o: Seeing the company's source code
Data rights cover your personal data, not company code.
Setting the company's prices
The law does not give this.
Asking the company to delete their data
Right. The right to erasure is one of the data subject rights.
Choosing which security tools the company must buy
Individuals do not choose the tools. The company must protect the data.

q.q: A service member posts a photo of a new badge, a base map and a deployment date on social media. What is the main risk?
o: The picture will use too much storage
Storage is not a privacy risk.
Strangers can piece it together for scams or stalking
Right. Small facts add up. Follow unit rules and keep privacy settings tight.
The platform will ban the account for posting too many photos
This may happen, but it is not the main privacy risk.
Friends will see an old photo
Seeing a photo is the intended use. The danger is who else sees it.

q.title: Read a suspicious email's details
q.scenario: A staff member forwarded a message that says their mailbox is disabled. You are authorized to read this copy of the message details from the mail gateway. The unit's real mail domain is unit.example.org. Mark every line that is a warning sign of phishing, then pick the best action.
q.ticket: Ticket 5521: user asks if the message about the mailbox is real. Review only this one message copy. Do not open the attachment or follow the link.

lines.why: The display name sounds official, but the address is not in unit.example.org. Attackers choose names that look like the real thing.
Replies would go to a free mail account, not the help desk. A real IT team answers from its own domain.
The sender checks all failed. The mail did not come from servers the claimed domain allows, which fits a forged sender.

lines.text: Subject: URGENT - mailbox disabled in 2 hours
lines.why: A short deadline and a threat are a pressure tactic. Phishers want you to act before you think.

lines.text: Body: Dear user, your mailbox is over quota. Sign in now or lose access.
lines.why: A generic greeting, a threat and a demand to sign in are common phishing signs. Your own IT team would use your name and a ticket.
The words shown and the real destination do not match. The real link goes to an outside look-alike site.
A small HTML file asking for a sign-in is a common trick to show a fake login page from your own computer.
An ordinary date line. It is neither good nor bad on its own.
The message is addressed to the staff member who reported it, which is normal.
This only says the message has several parts, such as text and an attachment. Almost every email has it.
A low spam score is not a warning sign by itself. It also does not prove the message is safe, so judge the other lines.

ask.label: What is the best action for this message?
opts: Report it as phishing through the unit's process and delete it without clicking
Open the attachment in a sandbox to see what it does
Reply to the sender and ask whether the message is real
Forward it to the whole team so they know what to avoid
ask.why: Reporting lets the security team block the sender and check for other recipients. Opening the attachment or replying is risky, and forwarding spreads the lure to more people.

q.title: Handle a flaw you found in a legal test
q.scenario: You joined a company's bug bounty program. The written rules name one test website as in scope. While testing it, you find a login page that can be bypassed with a crafted input. Add the steps in the order a responsible tester should follow. Some ideas do not belong.
q.ticket: Program rules: test only the listed site, do not read or copy real customer data, report through the program's private form.

rules.text: Check the written scope and rules before you test anything
rules.why: Written permission and scope make the test legal. Everything else depends on staying inside them.

rules.text: Stop at proof that the bypass works and do not read real user data
rules.why: A harmless proof is enough. Reading real data harms users and goes beyond what the program allows.

rules.text: Write down the steps, the time and the effect so the team can repeat it
rules.why: Clear notes help the owner confirm and fix the flaw quickly.

rules.text: Send the report privately to the program's contact
rules.why: A private report lets the owner fix the flaw before attackers learn about it.

rules.text: Give the team reasonable time to fix it and answer their questions
rules.why: Fixes take time. Staying in touch builds trust and keeps users safe while the work is done.

rules.text: Talk about the details in public only after the fix or the agreed date
rules.why: Public details are safe to share after the hole is closed, or when the program has agreed to a date.

rules.text: Download the customer table to show how serious the flaw is
rules.why: Taking real customer data is a privacy breach and breaks the program rules, even with good intent.

rules.text: Post the exploit on social media to pressure the vendor
rules.why: This puts every user at risk before a fix exists.

rules.text: Sell the flaw to the highest bidder
rules.why: Selling to unknown buyers can lead to attacks on real people and is the opposite of responsible handling.

before.why: Confirm what is allowed before you test, and keep the proof small.
Record what you did and saw once the proof is done.
A clear write-up comes before the report so the owner can act on it.
Allow time for a fix only after the owner has been told.

last.why: Public talk comes last, once the flaw is fixed or the agreed date has passed.

q.title: Find out why a workstation cannot reach the intranet
q.scenario: A user on PC22 can open nothing on the unit intranet by name. You are authorized to run basic checks on this one workstation, and a written approval is on the ticket. Work from the bottom up: address, gateway, address reach, then names. Fix the cause without scanning other systems.
q.ticket: INC-6102: intranet.example.org will not open on pc22 (10.20.5.22). Scope: this workstation only. No scanning of the network.
q.intro: pc22 (Ubuntu workstation, user analyst, sudo allowed). Type a command.

cmds.out:
2: eth0: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 state UP
    inet 10.20.5.22/24 brd 10.20.5.255 scope global eth0

default via 10.20.5.1 dev eth0
10.20.5.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 10.20.5.22

64 bytes from 10.20.5.1: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=0.6 ms
64 bytes from 10.20.5.1: icmp_seq=2 ttl=64 time=0.5 ms
--- 10.20.5.1 ping statistics ---
2 packets transmitted, 2 received, 0% packet loss

64 bytes from 10.20.1.5: icmp_seq=1 ttl=62 time=2.1 ms
64 bytes from 10.20.1.5: icmp_seq=2 ttl=62 time=2.0 ms
--- 10.20.1.5 ping statistics ---
2 packets transmitted, 2 received, 0% packet loss
ping: intranet.example.org: Temporary failure in name resolution

alt.out:
PING intranet.example.org (10.20.1.5) 56(84) bytes of data.
64 bytes from intranet.example.org (10.20.1.5): icmp_seq=1 ttl=62 time=2.1 ms
64 bytes from intranet.example.org (10.20.1.5): icmp_seq=2 ttl=62 time=2.0 ms

cmds.out:
;; communications error to 10.20.9.9#53: timed out
;; no servers could be reached
DNS server for eth0 set to 10.20.1.2
Nmap is not installed on this host. Your approval covers only this workstation, so no scans of the network or of other systems.

checks.why: The address 10.20.5.22/24 is set, so the first layer is fine. Always rule out the simple things first.

checks.t: Checked the gateway and that it answers
checks.why: The default gateway 10.20.5.1 is listed and answers a ping, so the local link and router are fine.

checks.t: Showed the server answers by IP address while the name fails
checks.why: Reaching 10.20.1.5 by number proves the path works. The failed name lookup narrows the fault to DNS.

checks.t: Found the DNS server the PC is set to use
checks.why: The PC points at 10.20.9.9, which does not answer. That is the cause.

checks.t: Proved the unit's DNS server answers
checks.why: Asking 10.20.1.2 directly returns the right address, so it is the server the PC should use.

checks.t: Pointed the PC at the working DNS server
checks.why: Setting the correct resolver fixes name lookups without touching any other system.
Your approval covers this workstation only. A network scan without written permission is out of scope and may be illegal.

q.title: Place the parts of a website's certificate trust chain
q.scenario: A browser must decide whether to trust a bank's website. Place each part in the right spot of the chain of trust. Three parts in the tray do not belong in a safe design.
q.ticket: Review PKI-04. Rules: the browser trusts only what is signed by a trusted root, and private keys never leave their owner.

slots.label: Spot A
slots.hint: self-signed and already installed in the browser or operating system

slots.label: Spot B
slots.hint: signed by the root; signs website certificates day to day so the root can stay offline

slots.label: Spot C
slots.hint: sent by the website at connection; holds the site name and its public key

slots.label: Spot D
slots.hint: never sent to anyone; proves the site owns the certificate

slots.label: Spot E
slots.hint: lets the browser ask if a certificate was cancelled

devs.name: Root CA certificate
devs.why: The root is the trust anchor. Browsers trust it because it ships in their store, and everything below is trusted through it.

devs.name: Intermediate CA certificate
devs.why: An intermediate signs the site certificates so the root private key can stay safely offline.

devs.name: Website X.509 certificate
devs.why: The site sends this at connection. It names the site, holds its public key and carries the CA's signature.

devs.name: Website private key
devs.why: Only the server holds it. Using it to prove ownership is what lets the browser trust the public key in the certificate.

devs.name: OCSP responder
devs.why: The browser can ask it whether a certificate was revoked, for example after a key theft.

devs.name: Private key on a public web page
devs.why: If anyone can download the key, anyone can pretend to be the site. A private key must never be shared.

devs.name: Self-signed bank certificate
devs.why: Nobody trusted vouches for it, so browsers warn. It cannot stand in for a CA-signed certificate on a public bank site.

devs.name: Visitor password hash
devs.why: A password hash belongs to the login system. It plays no part in the certificate chain.
